q1_issues.issue: (Meaning sk_clear_1 sk_have_1) coins a relation head from the participle 'meaning', which the reduced-relative rule forbids (the ban on (Concerning rule levy)) — 'meaning that P' must take the ordinary event form.
The content clause 'that they really hate Islam' is emitted as a free-floating hate bundle with no atom linking it to sk_evidence_1, so the evidence-of-what relation is simply lost.
The reified state (Member sk_clear_1 clear) (Experiencer sk_clear_1 sk_target_1) carries no deontic marker, so the sealed proposition says the target IS clear rather than that it must be.
(Manner sk_hate_1 really) mis-slots the intensifier 'really' into Manner, which the instruction set names as exactly the wrong move for an unrepresentable adverbial.
'should' is a strength-0.7 deontic, but a seal carries one outer TV, so the inner (Obligated sk_have_1) is indistinguishable from a full-force 'must'.

q2_gaps: noun-complement finite that-clause ('authentic evidence ... that they really hate Islam') — it is neither a propositional attitude nor a PP complement of a noun
an of-phrase on a noun that is neither a nominalization nor a true relational noun ('evidence of the target'); the 'photo of Mary' case is barred from Possession but given no positive encoding
degree/intensifier adverb modifying a verb ('really hate') — Degree is defined only over adjectives
first-person plural pronoun 'we' — the no-antecedent pronoun rule enumerates only he/she/they/it
graded truth values inside a seal: a sealed term has no per-conjunct TV, so a 0.7 deontic or a lowered confidence cannot be recorded
direct quotation as an attitude complement — the propositional-attitudes section covers finite 'that'-clauses only
a framing/domain PP scoping over a copular clause ('In jihad, the target must be clear') has no specified anchor; state reification is not one of the listed triggers
notes: The say/seal skeleton and the projection of the definite 'the target' to top level are handled correctly; the damage is all inside the single sealed term. The 'meaning that' clause and the evidence-content clause together account for most of the fidelity loss.
